section: Figure 3 — Validate inputs at the boundary
text:
Figure 3 — Validate inputs at the boundary
This example illustrates the principle behind Rule 4: uploaded files should be checked immediately after import, before downstream filtering, plotting, or enrichment.

R Shiny
raw_data <- reactive({
  req(input$file)
  df <- read.csv(input$file$datapath)
  required <- c("gene", "logFC", "adj.P.Val")
  validate(
    need(
      all(required %in% names(df)),
      "Uploaded file is missing required columns."
    )
  )
  df
})


Python Shiny
@reactive.calc
def raw_data():
    f = input.file()
    if f is None:
        return None
    df = pd.read_csv(f[0]["datapath"])
    required = ["gene", "logFC", "adj.P.Val"]
    missing = [c for c in required if c not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        return None
    return df

title: Golden Rules for Turning Bioinformatics Analyses into Interactive Web Applications
text:
Motivation
This project arose from the challenges in developing a web application for the project “Innovative Diagnostic Solutions for Viral-Induced Asthma: Towards Timely and Precise Paediatric Care”, funded by an Innovation Fellowship from the Future Health Research and Innovation (FHRI) Fund, Department of Health, Western Australia (IF2024-25/1). This manuscript draws on those experiences to offer ten practical rules, with the hope of saving others the planning effort and trial and error that inevitably accompany a first implementation.

title: Methods
text:
The manuscript is a Golden Rules paper, not a software benchmarking study. The R Shiny and Python Shiny applications are provided as worked examples to illustrate transferable design principles for turning a bioinformatics analysis into an interactive web application.
The worked example used throughout the manuscript is a differential gene expression and Gene Ontology enrichment application that allows users to upload a results table, explore thresholds interactively, visualise outputs, and download a report capturing the current analysis state.

title: Methods
text:
The manuscript is a Golden Rules paper, not a software benchmarking study. The R Shiny and Python Shiny applications are provided as worked examples to illustrate transferable design principles for turning a bioinformatics analysis into an interactive web application.
The worked example used throughout the manuscript is a differential gene expression and Gene Ontology enrichment application that allows users to upload a results table, explore thresholds interactively, visualise outputs, and download a report capturing the current analysis state.

title: Methods
text:
Validation dataset
The worked example uses GSE60450, a public mouse mammary gland RNA-seq dataset comparing luminal and basal cell populations across developmental stages.
This dataset was chosen because it is public, citable, and suitable for demonstrating a complete interactive workflow from differential expression results to downstream interpretation.
The reference input used by both applications is produced by Shiny_app/R/01_data_prep.R. The script downloads the gene-level counts and sample annotation from GEO, matches count columns to samples by sample name, keeps expressed genes with filterByExpr, applies TMM normalisation, and fits a limma-voom model with design ~ stage + celltype (virgin, pregnant and lactating stages; basal and luminal cells). The contrast reported is basal versus luminal, so a positive log2 fold change means higher expression in basal cells.

title: Methods
text:
GO enrichment
Both applications run over-representation analysis for the three GO ontologies and use every gene in the uploaded table as the background set. The R application uses clusterProfiler with the offline org.Mm.eg.db annotation. The Python application sends the gene lists to the Enrichr web service through gseapy. Because the annotation sources differ, the term lists are similar but not identical.
Full environment setup and data preparation steps are described on the Reproducibility page. Expanded paired code examples are provided on the Supplementary Code Examples page.

title: Methods
text:
Why both implementations are shown
The manuscript does not argue that one framework is universally superior. Instead, it uses both implementations to show that the same design principles can be applied across different ecosystems.
The practical choice between frameworks depends on the location of critical dependencies, the surrounding analytical environment, deployment constraints, and the needs of the intended users.

title: Methods
text:
Main practical differences
For the worked example in the manuscript, the most relevant differences are:

bioinformatics ecosystem maturity
offline versus internet-dependent enrichment
report-generation workflow
deployment and containerisation options

These trade-offs are summarised in Table 1 of the manuscript.

title: Reproducibility
text:
R application (Shiny_app/R)

Restore the environment
Package versions are locked in renv.lock:
Rscript -e "renv::restore()"
On a new machine you can instead install everything and write a new lockfile with:
Rscript 00_setup.R


Build the reference dataset
Rscript 01_data_prep.R
This downloads GSE60450 from GEO, runs limma-voom and writes data/GSE60450_limma.csv for both applications. It takes about two minutes on a laptop.


Run and test
Rscript -e "shiny::runApp()"
Rscript tests/testthat.R

title: Reproducibility
text:
Python application (Shiny_app/python)

Restore the environment
conda env create -f shiny_app_py_env.yml
conda activate shiny_app_py
or, without conda:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt


Run and test
shiny run app.py
pytest -q

title: Reproducibility
text:
Continuous integration and releases
Every push runs a version check, linting (lintr, ruff) and both test suites on GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml). Pushing a version tag such as v1.0.0 runs the release workflow: it repeats these checks, publishes Docker images of both applications to GitHub Container Registry, creates a GitHub Release from CHANGELOG.md, and redeploys both applications. Each release can be archived on Zenodo with its own DOI.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Troubleshooting

The uploaded file is rejected
The message names the missing or invalid column. Column names are case-sensitive: gene, logFC and adj.P.Val are required.


Python GO enrichment does not run
The Python application queries the Enrichr web service, so the server must have internet access. The other tabs and the download still work, and the report records that enrichment could not be run.


Results differ between R and Python
The two applications illustrate the same design principles with different libraries. GO term lists differ because the annotation sources differ (org.Mm.eg.db versus Enrichr). For the genomics example in the manuscript, the R application is the reference implementation.
